qualityBar.verdict: It moves like Doom and reads like Castlevania, and the moment the stairs to Dracula appear in first person it stops being a novelty.

expected.longDescription:
There is a long tradition of Doom total conversions that reuse the engine and little else, and Simon's Destiny is one of the best of them. Andrea Gori, who works as Batandy and is better known for the Golden Souls series, rebuilt the first Castlevania as six large first-person levels in GZDoom. Not a level pack with Castlevania textures — a reconstruction, with the original's structure, enemy roster, sub-weapon economy and boss order translated into rooms you walk through.

The translation is the interesting part. The whip becomes a short-reach melee weapon that punishes standing still, and the sub-weapons — axe, cross, holy water, dagger, stopwatch — keep their heart cost, so the resource loop from the NES game survives intact. Candles still break. Hearts still drop. The stairs are still there, and finding them in three dimensions instead of seeing them scroll past turns a piece of level furniture into an actual moment. Dracula still has two phases.

What GZDoom brings is verticality and pace. Doom's movement is fast and slippery in a way NES Castlevania emphatically was not, and rather than fight that, Gori built levels that use it: courtyards, towers, clock rooms with real height. It is closer to a Castlevania-flavoured Doom than a first-person Castlevania, and it is better for the choice.

Practically: the Windows build is self-contained, about 72 MB, and needs nothing else installed — no Doom, no Doom II, no WAD to supply. It reached version 1.4, which is the release to play. The engine underneath supports mouselook, gamepads and the usual GZDoom options, so the controls are as configurable as you want them.

The legal position is the same as every Castlevania fan work: Konami has not licensed it, and it survives because nobody has asked for it to stop. It has been publicly available since 2017 and updated since, which is longer than most.

We list it because it is a six-level game that a lot of people would enjoy and almost nobody stumbles across — it lives on Doom forums and itch.io, two places most players never look.
expected.whyWePickedIt: We picked Simon's Destiny because it is the kind of thing that only exists because someone wanted it to. Nobody was going to fund a first-person Castlevania, so a Doom modder built one, gave it away, and kept patching it for years. PlayBound exists to put work like that in front of people who would otherwise never see it — it is free, it is finished, it needs nothing else installed, and it is genuinely good rather than merely impressive-for-a-mod.
expected.thatOneThing: The whip is a Doom weapon now — short reach, real commitment, and holy water that behaves exactly as it did in 1987, thrown into a three-dimensional room.

installSteps.text: Download the self-contained Windows build. PlayBound's one-click install does this for you — you do not need Doom, Doom II or a separate GZDoom.
Extract the zip and run the GZDoom executable inside. Simon's Destiny is already selected as the game — there is nothing to configure.

faq.q: Do I need Doom or Doom II to play this?
faq.a: No. It is a standalone total conversion — all the art, sound and levels are original. The Windows build we link bundles the GZDoom engine, so nothing else is required.
Yes. Batandy has distributed it free since 2017 with no payment, account or donation required.

faq.q: Is this an official Konami game?
faq.a: No. It is an unlicensed fan project. Konami has neither endorsed nor sponsored it.

faq.q: Does it work with a controller?
faq.a: Yes. It runs on GZDoom, which has full gamepad support and remappable controls in its own options menu.

faq.q: How long is it, and which version should I play?
faq.a: Six levels, comfortably one evening. Version 1.4 is the latest and the one to play.

set.longDescription:
Simon's Destiny takes the route through the first Castlevania and rebuilds it as a first-person trip through Dracula's castle. Andrea Gori, working as Batandy, made six GZDoom levels around the rhythm of the NES game: whip enemies at close range, break candles for hearts, spend those hearts on sub-weapons, and keep climbing until the count himself runs out of places to hide. The result feels more like a deliberately designed game than a set of familiar textures on borrowed maps.

The camera changes the old fights. A whipping distance that looked obvious from the side becomes a risk you have to judge while moving toward a monster. An axe is suddenly a thrown object crossing a room with real height. Stairs are no longer a line you walk up while the screen scrolls; they are the way forward through a space you can inspect. The Doom engine gives Simon speed that the original never allowed, but the short reach of his main weapon still asks you to get uncomfortably close.

Batandy keeps enough of the 1987 game's structure for Castlevania fans to recognize the journey, while the rooms and first-person movement give Doom players something other than a costume change. The levels have their own courtyards, towers and interiors. It is a fan work, not a Konami release, and it does not offer multiplayer or a dedicated server. The point is one complete castle run with the usual GZDoom ability to save and adjust controls.

Installation deserves a clear warning. Batandy's current version 1.4 download is game data, not a Windows executable. We inspected the 75 MB ZIP used in the old PlayBound listing: it contains Castlevania.ipk3, a changelog and a README, with no GZDoom executable. The README instructs players to install GZDoom 3.7.1 or newer, put the IPK3 alongside it, and choose Simon's Destiny at launch with hardware OpenGL selected. You do not need a commercial Doom WAD. Until PlayBound has a tested engine-plus-game recipe, the download should open the developer's page and the steps should be manual. GZDoom has joystick configuration, but this particular game has not been controller-tested through PlayBound, so we are not promising a ready-to-play controller profile.

We keep Simon's Destiny in the catalog because the conversion has a specific idea and follows it all the way to Dracula. A first-person remake could have been a joke that ended after one corridor. Here the whip, candles, hearts and castle route hold together for a whole evening. The install needs honest instructions; the game itself rewards the effort.
set.whyWePickedIt: Six authored levels turn a familiar castle into a place you navigate from the inside. We like fan projects that follow one strong gameplay idea through to a complete game, and Simon's Destiny earns that place. We also want its install explained accurately: the free IPK3 needs the separate free GZDoom engine.
set.thatOneThing: An axe misses a bat, sails over the stair rail, and suddenly a 1987 sub-weapon has three dimensions of bad timing.

installSteps.text: Download version 1.4 from Batandy's itch.io page, then download GZDoom 3.7.1 or newer from zdoom.org. The game ZIP contains Castlevania.ipk3, not an executable.
Place Castlevania.ipk3 in the GZDoom folder, run GZDoom, select Castlevania: Simon's Destiny in its game chooser and select Hardware (OpenGL) rendering. No Doom or Doom II WAD is required.
In the game's player options, enable Always Autorun. Configure movement, primary fire, secondary fire, jump, crouch and use to taste.

faq.q: Do I need Doom or Doom II?
faq.a: No commercial Doom WAD is required. You do need the separate, free GZDoom engine; the Simon's Destiny ZIP contains only the Castlevania.ipk3 game data plus text files.

faq.q: Does PlayBound install it in one click?
faq.a: Not yet. The previous listing incorrectly claimed the linked ZIP bundled GZDoom. Follow Batandy's installation instructions until an engine-plus-game recipe has been tested.

faq.q: Is it an official Castlevania game?
faq.a: No. It is an unlicensed, nonprofit fan game by Batandy and is not endorsed by Konami.
GZDoom offers joystick settings, but PlayBound has not verified this game's bindings or a controller profile. Keyboard and mouse are the documented setup.
No multiplayer mode or server package is documented for Simon's Destiny; this listing is for its single-player campaign.
